title: A-N-H
hook: anah, to answer, and ani, the poor or humble

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-A-L: sha'al, to ask, Hannah's asking and the child who can't ask yet. Your line was ask. What did you ask, and what came back? Today, the other half of a question. Day one thousand four hundred nine.

Someone snaps at you. A text in capitals, a remark across the table, a customer who's had a long day and decided you're the reason. You have about one second before you answer. Proverbs has a line for that second: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." The Hebrew for answer there is ma'aneh, from the root ayin, nun, hey. And those same letters, read another way, give a word for someone poor, low, bowed down. An answer, and a humble person. Today's root holds both.
screen: `SOMEONE SNAPS AT YOU.` → `A SOFT ANSWER TURNETH AWAY WRATH.` → `THE SAME LETTERS: THE LOWLY.`

segments.voice: A-N-H. Ayin, nun, hey. Turn it three ways. First, to answer: anah. It's the everyday verb for replying, and also for God answering. In the Psalms: "This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him." The word for poor there is ani, written with the same letters. It isn't the ani that means I; that one starts with a different letter, alef. This ani is the poor one, the lowly, the one with nothing to bargain with. And the Psalm says that one is heard. Second, humility. From the same letters comes anav, humble, and anavah, humility. The Torah uses it for Moses, of all people, the leader who spoke with God: "Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth." Meek, there, is anav. The text doesn't call him the smartest or the strongest. It calls him the humblest. Third, the honest part. Dictionaries often list answering and being lowly as two separate roots that happen to share letters. Whether they were ever one word is a question for linguists. So the link isn't a hidden code. But some readers hear them together anyway, and the pairing teaches something: the soft answer is the humble answer. It doesn't need to win. It doesn't arrive with a speech prepared. It answers the way Moses led, from low down, without needing the last word. And the Psalm adds the other side: the one who is low is the one whose cry gets answered.
screen: `ANAH: TO ANSWER.` · `ANI: THE POOR ONE IS HEARD.` · `ANAV: MOSES, VERY MEEK.` · `TWO ROOTS, OR ONE? READERS DIFFER.` · then, large: `THE SOFT ANSWER IS THE HUMBLE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer someone humbly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a conversation that's waiting for your reply. An email you've been drafting in your head. An argument that's still warm. Someone who asked you something hard. Notice the answer you want to give, the one that wins. Let it sit for a breath. Then look for a softer one. Not weaker. Lower. An answer that leaves room for the other person. Maybe it starts with you might be right, or I didn't see it that way, tell me more. Hold that answer ready. If you pray, you can bring the person into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
screen: `A REPLY THAT'S WAITING.` · `THE ANSWER THAT WINS.` · `NOW A LOWER ONE.`

segments.voice: A-N-H. Ayin, nun, hey: anah, to answer; ma'aneh, an answer; ani, the poor one; anav, the humble. Today's word.
Your line: answer humbly. Today, when someone comes at you sharp, take one breath and give the softer answer. See what it turns away. Day one thousand four hundred nine.

howItsDone: Jewish ethical teaching prizes anavah, humility, and holds up Moses as its model from Numbers 12:3; Proverbs' 'soft answer' is a common Jewish guide for replying in a quarrel.

original.note: Hebrew: humble, the word used for Moses, in Numbers 12:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: a humble answer is a weak answer.
what it means: the soft answer turns away wrath, and the poor one's cry is the one that's answered.
what a scholar hears: anah, to answer, and anah, to be low, are often listed as two homonymous roots; the pairing is a reader's, not a proof.

notes: Proverbs 15:1, Psalms 34:6 (JPS 34:7) and Numbers 12:3 quoted from KJV. Confirm wording.
The script says the text calls Moses 'the humblest': this paraphrases 'very meek, above all the men ... upon the face of the earth' (Numbers 12:3), which the text says directly. Confirm the gloss.

Root honesty: ענה I (answer) and ענה II/III (be low, afflicted; ani, anav) are usually treated as separate homonymous roots; the script says so and frames the link as a reading, not etymology. Anav (with final vav) is often analyzed as from the same 'be low' root; the original note avoids the root question.
Ani (poor, with ayin) vs ani (I, with alef): stated; confirm.
